chunks.content: INTRODUCTION The ABO blood group system, discovered over a century ago, holds critical clinical significance in transfusion medicine and transplantation due to its potent immunogenicity. Accurate ABO typing is paramount, as errors may trigger life-threatening transfusion reactions. While conventional serology identifies major ABO types, approximately 0.01% of the population exhibits ABO subgroups, characterized by attenuated antigen expression . Molecular studies have elucidated that weakened A/B antigen expression primarily arises from three mechanisms – : 1) missense variants in the ABO gene coding region; 2) regulatory variants affecting transcription in the promoter and first intron (+5.8 kb site); 3) rare heterozygous alleles. The International Society of Blood Transfusion (ISBT) database catalogs over 300 ABO alleles, yet >90% of subgroup mechanisms involve mutations within the glycosyltransferase domain. Notably, no large genomic deletion (>5 kb) in the ABO promoter upstream region has been documented to cause antigen attenuation. This knowledge gap impedes a comprehensive understanding of ABO regulation and limits molecular diagnostic precision. In this study, we investigated a Chinese pedigree with hereditary Aweak phenotype using serological analysis and third-generation single-molecule sequencing. We report for the first time a 12,309bp deletion variant upstream of the ABO promoter that reduces A antigen expression. This largest regulatory deletion identified to date co-segregated with attenuated A antigen expression across three generations. Our discovery expands the molecular mechanistic spectrum of ABO subgroups and highlights the necessity of screening for non-coding structural variants in cases with aberrant serological results. MATERIALS AND METHODS Blood samples The proband was a 36-year-old male of Hui ethnicity, a voluntary blood donor from Ningxia region with no history of blood transfusion. This was his first participation in voluntary blood donation. Routine ABO blood typing revealed a forward and reverse typing discrepancy. Further molecular biological testing was performed, and family analysis was conducted involving his parents, wife, two daughters, and son. All participants signed informed consent forms. Instruments and reagents ABO forward typing reagents: Shanghai Blood Center (Batch No.: 20230301); ABO reverse typing reagents: Shanghai Blood Center (Batch No.: 20240507); Human whole blood genomic DNA extraction kit: Tiangen Biotech Co. Ltd., Beijing, China (Batch No.: A0321A); Red blood cell genotyping detection kit - single-molecule real-time sequencing: Xi’an Haorui Gene Technology Co. Ltd., Shaanxi, China (Batch No.: 20240803); Quality control reagent - Qubit dsDNA BR Assay Kit: Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA (Batch No.: 2896576); Library preparation reagents - Sequel II Binding Kit 3.2 and Cleanup Beads: PacBio, Menlo Park, CA, USA (Batch No.: 033315); Sequencing reagents - Sequel II Sequencing Kit: PacBio (Batch No.: 131032); Sequencing chip - SMRT Cell 8M Tray: PacBio (Batch No.: 420402); PCR amplification reagent - PrimeSTAR GXL DNA Polymerase: Takara Bio Inc., Shiga, Japan (Batch No.: R050Q); PCR Thermal Cycler: Thermo Fisher Scientific (Model: A47394); Gel Imaging System: Bio-Rad, Hercules, CA, USA (Model: Gel Doc 76S); Sequencing Instrument - PacBio Sequel II System: PacBio (Model: 64066). Serological tests ABO forward/reverse typing and adsorption-elution tests were performed in strict accordance with the National Clinical Laboratory Procedures (4 th Edition) operational standards. Cell grouping (forward typing): monoclonal anti-A, anti-B, anti-A,B, and anti-H reagents (Shanghai Blood Biopharmaceutical Co. Ltd., Shanghai, China) were used. Testing was performed by the tube method in saline medium. Agglutination strength was recorded on a semi-quantitative scale from 0 to 4+. Serum typing (reverse grouping): commercial A1, B, and O group reagent red cells (Shanghai Blood Biopharmaceutical Co. Ltd.) were used. Testing was performed by the saline tube method. Adsorption-elution test : this test was conducted on the proband and pedigree members with the Aweak phenotype to confirm weak A antigen expression. Briefly, an equal volume of titer-standardized human anti-A serum was added to washed, packed red blood cells for adsorption at 4°C for 1 hour. Following extensive washing, antibody elution was performed at 56°C for 10 minutes. The resulting eluate was then tested against A1 and O red cells via the indirect antiglobulin test. Genomic DNA extraction Genomic DNA was extracted from 300 μL of whole blood using the Blood Genomic DNA Extraction Kit (Cat. No. 70423-10 [Suzhou Beaver, Suzhou Industrial Park, China]). <italic toggle="yes">ABO</italic> gene amplification Designed 4 pairs of primers to amplify the full length of the ABO gene and its promoter upstream region. Multiplex PCR amplification was performed using PrimeSTAR GXL DNA Polymerase (R050Q [Takara Bio Inc.]) on a PCR thermal cycler under the following program: 94°C for 2 min (1 cycle); 98°C for 12 sec, 68°C for 12 min (27 cycles); 68°C for 10 min (1 cycle). This yielded the full-length ABO gene sequence and its distal promoter upstream sequence ( , ). The PCR products underwent concentration measurement using the Qubit dsDNA BR Assay Kit ( Q32854 [Thermo Fisher Scientific]) and quality control via agarose gel electrophoresis. Qualified samples proceeded to library construction. Library construction The library construction system contained 4

Multiplex PCR amplification was performed using PrimeSTAR GXL DNA Polymerase (R050Q [Takara Bio Inc.]) on a PCR thermal cycler under the following program: 94°C for 2 min (1 cycle); 98°C for 12 sec, 68°C for 12 min (27 cycles); 68°C for 10 min (1 cycle). This yielded the full-length ABO gene sequence and its distal promoter upstream sequence ( , ). The PCR products underwent concentration measurement using the Qubit dsDNA BR Assay Kit ( Q32854 [Thermo Fisher Scientific]) and quality control via agarose gel electrophoresis. Qualified samples proceeded to library construction. Library construction The library construction system contained 4 μL PCR products. 2μL SMRTBELL ADAPTER INDEX PLATE 96A (102009200 [Pacbio]), 1 μL DNase/RNase-Free Deionized Water, 0.5 μL 100 mM ATP (NE, N0440 [New England Biolabs, Ipswich, MA, USA]), 0.5 μL 10 mM dNTP (NEB, N0447 [New England Biolabs]), 0.5 μL (5U) T4 Polynucleotide Kinase (NEB, M0236 [New England Biolabs]), 0.5 μL (1.5U) T4 DNA Polymerase (NEB, M0203 [New England Biolabs]) and 1 μL (400U) T4 DNA Ligase (NEB, M0202 [New England Biolabs]), a total of 10 μL reaction mixture. The reaction mixture was subjected to adapter ligation under the following conditions: 37°C for 20 min; 25°C for 15 min; 65°C for 10 min. Each sample was ligated with a unique barcode adapter for specific identification. Subsequently, 1.5 μL (7.5 U) Exonuclease I (Cat. No. M006 [Novoprotein, Beijing, China]) and 0.5 μL (50 U) Exonuclease III (Cat. No. M007 [Novoprotein]) were added to digest unligated products at 37°C for 60 min. The reaction was purified with 0.45× VAHTS DNA Clean Beads (Cat. No. N411-01 [Vazyme, Nanjing, China]) to obtain the final library. Libraby preparation The sequencing primer (Binding Kit 3.2 and Cleanup Beads, Cat. No. 102-333-300 [PacBio]) was added to the library, followed by incubation at 20°C for 30 min to allow primer annealing to the adapter sequences. Subsequently, the sequencing enzyme (Binding Kit 3.2 and Cleanup Beads, Cat. No. 102-333-300 [PacBio]) was introduced, and the mixture was incubated at 30°C for 30 min to immobilize the enzyme onto the primers. The final sequencing-ready library was obtained via magnetic bead purification. Library sequencing The sequencing-ready library was loaded onto a SMRT Cell and sequenced using the PacBio Sequel II high-throughput sequencing platform. The SMRT Cell contains 8 million zero-mode waveguide (ZMW) nanostructures, each designed to capture a single circular DNA molecule. Within each ZMW, DNA templates bound with sequencing primers and immobilized enzymes are anchored. During sequencing, fluorescently labeled dNTPs (each nucleotide tagged with a distinct fluorophore) are introduced. The sequencing enzyme incorporates complementary dNTPs into the nascent strand through base pairing. Upon incorporation of each nucleotide, the attached fluorophore is excited by a specific laser wavelength, emitting a characteristic fluorescence signal. These signals are detected in real time by the instrument and computationally translated into base calls, generating the final DNA sequence. Data analysis Sequence alignment analysis was performed using SnapGene software (Dotmatics, Boston, MA, USA) against the reference sequence ABO*A1.01 to identify mutation sites. The detected variants were then classified according to the Blood Group Antigen Gene Mutation Database (maintained by the International Society of Blood Transfusion, ISBT) to determine the blood group phenotype. RESULTS Serological results In forward typing, the red blood cells of the proband, his father, and his son all exhibited a mixed-field agglutination appearance (2+mf) with both anti-A and anti-A,B reagents. No agglutination was observed with anti-B, while a strong (4+) reaction was seen with anti-H. The reverse typing results were consistent with type A, and the positive adsorption-elution tests confirmed the specific presence of weak A antigens on the red cells of all three individuals, confirming their Aweak subtype. His mother and daughter 2 were both blood group O. His wife and daughter 1 were both blood group B ( ). Third-generation single-molecule sequencing results Sequencing analysis of the proband and his family revealed that one haplotype allele of the ABO gene in the proband, his father, and his son carried a 12309-bp deletion upstream of the promoter region on the basis of the normal ABO*A1.02 allele. The other haplotype harbored a normal O allele ( ABO*O.01.01* or *ABO*O.01.02* ). The genotypes of his mother, wife, daughter 1, and daughter 2 were ( , ): Mother: ABO*O.01.01/ABO*O.01.01 (homozygous), Wife: ABO*B.01/ABO*O.01.02 , Daughter 1: ABO*B.01/ABO*O.01.01 , Daughter 2: ABO*O.01.01/ABO*O.01.02 . No variants were detected in the coding regions, introns, or splice sites of the ABO gene. The locations and nucleotide changes in key variant sites are shown in . Pedigree analysis of the proband The ABO*A1.02 allele carrying the 12.3-kb deletion was inherited by the proband from his father and subsequently transmitted to his son, as demonstrated in . DISCUSSION ABO antigen expression is indirectly controlled by three principal alleles (A, B, and O), which determine the specificity and density of antigens on red

, ): Mother: ABO*O.01.01/ABO*O.01.01 (homozygous), Wife: ABO*B.01/ABO*O.01.02 , Daughter 1: ABO*B.01/ABO*O.01.01 , Daughter 2: ABO*O.01.01/ABO*O.01.02 . No variants were detected in the coding regions, introns, or splice sites of the ABO gene. The locations and nucleotide changes in key variant sites are shown in . Pedigree analysis of the proband The ABO*A1.02 allele carrying the 12.3-kb deletion was inherited by the proband from his father and subsequently transmitted to his son, as demonstrated in . DISCUSSION ABO antigen expression is indirectly controlled by three principal alleles (A, B, and O), which determine the specificity and density of antigens on red blood cell surfaces, thereby establishing distinct blood group phenotypes. In 1990, Yamamoto et al . successfully cloned the cDNA sequence of the A101 allele, providing the first molecular-level explanation of the ABO blood group system. Subsequently, in 1994, Yamamoto et al. identified that the ABO gene mutation c.1054C>T reduces glycosyltransferase activity, elucidating the molecular mechanism underlying attenuated antigen expression in subgroups . Inheritance of the ABO blood group gene follows Mendelian principles. The ABO gene spans approximately 19.5 kb, comprising 7 exons and 6 introns. Its 1065-bp coding sequence primarily resides in exons 6 and 7 (823 bp), which encode the core catalytic domain of the glycosyltransferase protein. Notably, 98% of pathogenic mutations cluster within exons 6 and 7 . Additional regulatory elements include the 5’ and 3’ regulatory regions and intronic regions (e.g., intron 1). The phenotypic variation observed in ABO subgroups is primarily attributed to single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) . This study identifies for the first time an Aweak subtype in a Chinese blood donor family, resulting from a large 12.3 kb distal deletion upstream of the ABO gene ( ABO*A1.02 , c.1-13204_c.1-896del). The congruence was exact between the serological profile (weak agglutination, strong H, positive adsorption-elution) and the molecular data (intact coding region but the upstream deletion). This deletion co-segregated perfectly with the phenotype in three family members and was absent in those with normal typing. With long-read sequencing excluding other potential variants in the coding and regulatory regions, this distal deletion is confirmed as the direct cause of the attenuated A antigen expression. Our findings carry dual significance for transfusion safety. First, they elucidate the etiology of a novel category of problematic blood groups. When serology presents as Aweak with positive adsorption-elution tests, yet conventional molecular screening of the coding and core promoter regions reveals no abnormalities, the presence of a large upstream deletion such as this should be strongly suspected. Second, our results provide precise guidance for the clinical transfusion management of such individuals. For the individual as a blood donor: If misclassified as group O and transfused to an O recipient, the donor’s red blood cells, which still express trace A antigen, can react with the recipient’s anti-A antibodies, potentially triggering a delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction. Therefore, their blood must be labeled as an A subgroup and transfused to type-A recipients (with special notation). In our study, the proband’s initial donation was routinely misclassified as O. Discrepancy was identified upon reverse typing, and subsequent adsorption-elution testing and molecular diagnosis confirmed the Aweak subtype, thereby averting a mistransfusion risk. This case underscores that for blood donors exhibiting weak antigen expression or forward/reverse typing discrepancies, it is imperative to supplement with adsorption-elution tests and employ long-read sequencing for full-gene ABO analysis, establishing a combined “serology + molecular” identification protocol. For the individual as a patient: their blood group must be accurately identified as an A subgroup. When transfusion is required, the safest choice is either O-type washed red blood cells or blood of the identical A subgroup to avoid hemolytic reactions from high-titer anti-A in donor plasma. Additionally, since their serum may contain low-titer anti-A1 antibodies, extreme caution is warranted when transfusing plasma-rich components like A-type platelets; in such cases, AB-type blood products are the preferred choice. ABO gene expression is under the precise control of complex upstream regulatory elements. The core promoter is responsible for basal transcription, and its activity is distally regulated by elements such as enhancers and silencers , . These elements fine-tune transcription through chromatin remodeling and three-dimensional genome architecture, notably via enhancer-promoter looping. The large deletion identified in our study likely removes several cis-regulatory elements that are critical for high-level ABO expression in erythroid cells. These may include – : tissue-specific enhancer(s); clusters of binding sites for key erythroid transcription factors such as GATA1 and KLF1; regions that maintain an open chromatin state; elements that insulate the ABO promoter from the influence of adjacent repressive chromatin domains; alterations to the three-dimensional chromatin structure. By disrupting the function of these elements and/or altering the local chromatin environment, this large deletion ultimately leads to a significant reduction in the transcriptional level of the A gene in erythroid cells, thereby manifesting as weakened A

removes several cis-regulatory elements that are critical for high-level ABO expression in erythroid cells. These may include – : tissue-specific enhancer(s); clusters of binding sites for key erythroid transcription factors such as GATA1 and KLF1; regions that maintain an open chromatin state; elements that insulate the ABO promoter from the influence of adjacent repressive chromatin domains; alterations to the three-dimensional chromatin structure. By disrupting the function of these elements and/or altering the local chromatin environment, this large deletion ultimately leads to a significant reduction in the transcriptional level of the A gene in erythroid cells, thereby manifesting as weakened A antigen expression on the red blood cell membrane. Currently, the mechanisms known to cause weak A antigen expression are primarily concentrated on missense mutations, small insertions/deletions, or splice-site mutations within the ABO gene coding region – , which directly impair the structure and function of the A transferase. Recent studies have also identified point mutations in the core promoter region that can diminish promoter activity, leading to weakened antigen expression , .In contrast, the mechanism identified in our study is distinctly different: the variant is located distally upstream of the promoter (>10 kb), is a rare large genomic deletion, and its mode of action involves the long-range disruption of the gene regulatory network, rather than a direct effect on the enzyme protein or the core promoter. This finding provides novel insight into the molecular genetic basis of ABO subgroups. The success of this study is attributed to the application of third-generation single-molecule long-read sequencing. Its ultra-long reads enable seamless spanning of complex structural variation regions, and its unbiased whole-genome sequencing strategy ensures the accurate detection of large deletions hidden distally upstream of the gene , . This highlights the unique value of this technology in resolving challenging serological cases that are intractable with conventional methods. Our findings have clear implications for transfusion safety. For individuals exhibiting an A subgroup phenotype with discordant routine serological and genotyping results, screening for large deletions upstream of the ABO gene should be considered to achieve a precise diagnosis. We acknowledge that this study has limitations, primarily the lack of in vitro functional validation. Future research directions include: constructing reporter gene vectors to quantitatively assess the impact of this deletion on transcriptional activity; utilizing gene-editing technologies to validate its function in an endogenous model; and screening for the frequency of this variant in larger cohorts of individuals with A subgroups. CONCLUSIONS This study not only reports a novel mechanism for weakened A antigen expression caused by a large 12,309 bp deletion upstream of the ABO gene, but more importantly, by integrating detailed serological characterization with third-generation sequencing technology, we successfully resolved a challenging case with serological and genotypic discrepancies and established a clear clinical pathway for the precise transfusion management of such individuals. This deepens our understanding of the complex regulation of the ABO gene and highlights the significant value of translating advanced genomic discoveries into transfusion safety practice. This finding expands the spectrum of variants causing weakened ABO antigens from the traditional coding region and proximal promoter to distal regulatory regions, deepening the understanding of the complex regulatory network governing ABO gene expression and providing a new scientific basis for precise blood typing and transfusion safety.

chunks.content: Abbreviations PAS platelet additive solution PLT platelets PR Pathogen reduced RBC red blood cell TRALI Transfusion Related Acute Lung Injury WB Whole blood 1 INTRODUCTION Transfusion‐related acute lung injury (TRALI) is an uncommon but serious transfusion complication, marked by sudden‐onset respiratory distress and bilateral pulmonary edema that cannot be fully explained by circulatory overload or other underlying causes. , , , The widely accepted “two‐hit” model proposes that TRALI arises from two sequential events. The first hit involves recipient‐specific factors—systemic inflammation, underlying disease, or recent surgical trauma—that prime neutrophils and the pulmonary endothelium. , , , The second hit is the transfusion itself: biologically active donor mediators, most often antibodies against human leukocyte antigens (HLA) or human neutrophil antigens (HNA), trigger an acute inflammatory cascade that produces capillary leak, pulmonary edema, and hypoxemia. , , , During the past two decades, blood centers have adopted multiple mitigation strategies, especially for plasma and apheresis platelets, to reduce the likelihood that donor units contain HLA or HNA antibodies. , , One well‐established approach is preferential collection from male donors or from females who have never been pregnant or have tested negative for HLA/HNA antibodies. Thanks largely to these policies, the combined incidence of TRALI across all components is now generally below 1 per 100,000 transfused units. , , Less is known about platelet components, whether apheresis or whole‐blood‐derived, because donor screening measures are often layered with manufacturing changes aimed at decreasing immunologic risk. , , , , Platelet‐additive solutions (PAS) replace a substantial portion of plasma—often leaving ~35%—and should theoretically lower TRALI risk by decreasing exposure to antibody‐containing plasma. Pathogen‐reduction (PR) technologies such as INTERCEPT further modify platelets by inactivating pathogens and leukocytes. Yet robust, real‐world data comparing TRALI incidence among platelets in PAS, PR platelets, platelets stored entirely in plasma, and pooled whole‐blood‐derived platelets is lacking. In the United States, pooled platelets derived from whole blood (WB) remain in use at some centers and do not undergo the same stringent donor screening as apheresis platelets or plasma. Because each pool combines contributions—and residual plasma—from multiple donors, the probability of introducing a clinically significant HLA or HNA antibody may be multiplied. Although fatal TRALI has been reported even with red‐cell units that contain only small amounts of plasma, , it remains unclear what the relative risk of a pool of typically 5‐donor platelets is compared to apheresis platelets manufactured with current mitigation strategies. The few component‐specific estimates that exist highlight both progress and persistent uncertainty due to relatively small data sets. Vossoughi et al. surveyed five regional blood centers in nine Eastern and Midwestern states, reporting TRALI rates per 100,000 distributed units that fell from 6.4, 2.2, and 3.2 in 2007 for plasma, red blood cells, and platelets, respectively, to 0.43, 0.59, and 1.4 by 2017. The authors emphasized that heterogeneous platelet preparations and varied mitigation practices hampered precise risk assessment. Mowla et al. reported relative risk results from only ~215 participating hospitals of the CDC hemovigilance network grouping a range of adjudications from possible to probable TRALI cases from only 1.2 million apheresis units and ~525 k WB platelets. Gaps in knowledge therefore remain: we still lack contemporary, evidence‐based TRALI rates for specific platelet products (pooled vs. apheresis, PAS vs. PR vs. plasma) and for whole‐blood components manufactured under current US practices. Leveraging the uniquely large and detailed American Red Cross (ARC) database—encompassing nationwide distribution numbers and linked transfusion‐reaction reports—we aim to (1) determine component‐specific TRALI rates across modern platelet and plasma preparations, (2) quantify the contribution of manufacturing and donor‐selection variables, and (3) identify residual high‐risk scenarios that could inform targeted mitigation. Accurate, component‐level TRALI estimates will guide clinicians and patients in transfusion decisions, support researchers designing interventional studies, and help policymakers refine donor‐selection criteria and product‐manufacturing standards, ultimately reducing the residual burden of TRALI in US transfusion practice. 2 METHODS 2.1 Data source American Red Cross hemovigilance program. Between 2006 and 2023, the American Red Cross distributed 92,709,018 units of RBCs, 23,492,563 units of plasma, 2,206,615 units of cryoprecipitate, 16,961,599 units of platelets, of which 875,433 pooled whole‐blood‐derived platelets in plasma (PLT pooled, five donors per pool), which were pooled with five units in each pool, 11,672,537 apheresis‐plasma platelets (PLT plasma), 1,502,332 apheresis PAS platelets (PLT PAS), and 2,911,297 PR platelets in PAS (PLT PAS‐PR). No reports of TRALI related to cryoprecipitate were submitted. 2.2 Definitions and inclusion criteria Suspected transfusion reactions, reported by hospitals, consistent with TRALI across these blood products were evaluated by the Red Cross physicians (medical directors) according to the Canadian Consensus Conference (CCC) definition and classified as TRALI or possible TRALI on a 6‐point probability scale (P1–P6). , Our physicians use both serologic and clinical results from cases to assign the imputability designation to each reported TRALI diagnosis. These cases were recorded in the

(PLT plasma), 1,502,332 apheresis PAS platelets (PLT PAS), and 2,911,297 PR platelets in PAS (PLT PAS‐PR). No reports of TRALI related to cryoprecipitate were submitted. 2.2 Definitions and inclusion criteria Suspected transfusion reactions, reported by hospitals, consistent with TRALI across these blood products were evaluated by the Red Cross physicians (medical directors) according to the Canadian Consensus Conference (CCC) definition and classified as TRALI or possible TRALI on a 6‐point probability scale (P1–P6). , Our physicians use both serologic and clinical results from cases to assign the imputability designation to each reported TRALI diagnosis. These cases were recorded in the American Red Cross hemovigilance program for surveillance of blood donor and transfusion recipient complications. The operational changes in 2007 that were required for distributing predominantly male‐donor plasma were previously described. Cases involving transfusion of a single component type (e.g., plasma unit[s] only) are included in the primary analysis. Cases involving transfusion of more than one component type (e.g., RBC and plasma units) were excluded because of the uncertainty in attributing causation to a specific transfusion source when multiple component types (e.g., plasma and RBCs) were transfused within 6 hours of the reaction. , High‐probability or definite cases were coded as P5 or P6 by the regional medical directors and assigned the final classification. Low‐probability cases are rescinded by the hospital (P1) or do not support a diagnosis of TRALI or possible TRALI (P2) or more likely reflect other conditions (P3). Indeterminate (P4) cases cannot exclude TRALI or possible TRALI, but the clinical information does not meet the CCC definition (e.g., circulatory overload is present before transfusion, or the volume status is not well defined or documented). High‐probability cases are consistent with TRALI or possible TRALI according to the CCC definition and coded as P5 if a donor was not implicated or a HLA/HNA antibody‐containing component was not involved, or P6 if a donor was implicated (i.e., donor HLA‐antibody is a cognate or cross‐reactive [CREG]‐match for the patient's HLA type or a donor HNA‐antibody specificity is identified). The routine coding system does not distinguish TRALI from possible TRALI, which are collectively referred to as “high‐probability TRALI” or “probable TRALI” although reported clinical details are captured in our system. The presence (possible TRALI) or absence (TRALI) of alternate risk factors for the acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), such as sepsis, pneumonia, cardiopulmonary bypass, or trauma, is described separately for all high‐probability cases. For the present study on TRALI incidence, only cases classified as P5 and P6—those considered highly probable or definite—were included, ensuring a stronger correlation with transfusion as the underlying cause. 2.3 Platelet components: For the purposes of our analysis, we categorized platelets as follows 100% plasma apheresis platelets (Plasma PLT) PAS platelets (Apheresis stored in platelet‐additive solution) PAS‐PR platelets (Apheresis stored in platelet‐additive solution with pathogen reduction) Pooled platelets (whole‐blood‐derived, with five units combined into one “pool”, each containing a residual plasma of approximately 50 mL) 2.4 Statistical analysis We calculated the incidence of high‐probability TRALI per million distributions (10 6 units shipped to hospitals). Data for platelet products were separated into two epochs (2006–2016 and 2017–2023) to reflect the gradual adoption of pathogen reduction and the transition from 100% plasma to PAS as well as aligning results to adoption of required TRALI mitigation strategies. Linear mixed modeling, with product type as the fixed effect and distribution year as the random effect, was applied to detect significant differences in TRALI rates among product types over time. 3 RESULTS 3.1 Component distributions and overall <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">TRALI</styled-content> surveillance During the 18‐year surveillance period (2006–2023), the American Red Cross (ARC) distributed more than 92.7 million red blood cell (RBC) units, 23.5 million plasma units, and ~ 17 million platelet units (Table ). Implementation of two sequential mitigation measures occurred during this surveillance period—conversion to predominantly male‐donor plasma in 2005–2006 and introduction of HLA‐antibody testing for all previously pregnant female apheresis‐platelet donors in calendar year 2016. , ARC physicians investigated 268 suspected TRALI cases in the pre‐mitigation baseline year (2006) and an average of 247 suspected cases per year in the post‐mitigation era (2008–2023). Of these, 393 reports (~76.0%) met the program's “high probability” definition after centralized medical review. Annual high‐probability case counts fell steadily for plasma but remained relatively stable for RBCs and platelets. 3.2 Incidence trends by component High‐probability TRALI incidence per 1,000,000 distributed units is summarized in Table . The rate associated with plasma fell sharply—from 20.1 cases/10 6 units in 2006 to 5.4/10 6 cases by 2008—and has remained below 4/10 6 cases since 2012. No comparable decline was seen for RBCs, whose incidence persisted at 0.7–4.3/10 6 cases across the entire study interval, consistent with the absence of targeted TRALI‐mitigation strategies for RBC components. Platelet‐related TRALI demonstrated marked heterogeneity. Before 2016, the hierarchy of risk was pooled whole‐blood‐derived

fell steadily for plasma but remained relatively stable for RBCs and platelets. 3.2 Incidence trends by component High‐probability TRALI incidence per 1,000,000 distributed units is summarized in Table . The rate associated with plasma fell sharply—from 20.1 cases/10 6 units in 2006 to 5.4/10 6 cases by 2008—and has remained below 4/10 6 cases since 2012. No comparable decline was seen for RBCs, whose incidence persisted at 0.7–4.3/10 6 cases across the entire study interval, consistent with the absence of targeted TRALI‐mitigation strategies for RBC components. Platelet‐related TRALI demonstrated marked heterogeneity. Before 2016, the hierarchy of risk was pooled whole‐blood‐derived platelets (PLT pooled)—14.9/10 6 >100% plasma apheresis platelets (PLT plasma)—6.6/10 6 > distributions of apheresis platelets suspended in platelet‐additive solution (PLT PAS)—0/10 6 distributions (after excluding an outlier value for 2013). Linear mixed‐model analysis (fixed effect = platelet type; random effect = calendar year) confirmed a significant overall effect of platelet category on incidence ( p < .01). Pair‐wise contrasts showed PLT pooled to carry a 9–13‐fold higher risk than any apheresis preparation (all p ≤ .01). Following universal HLA screening of female platelet donors in 2016 and the progressive shift away from 100% plasma formulations, TRALI incidence from apheresis platelets declined by ~70%. There was a notable decrease in TRALI incidence in apheresis‐platelet products containing less plasma—particularly when pathogen reduction was also employed (PAS‐PR). However, this decrease was not as dramatic as initially anticipated, suggesting that removal of plasma alone confers only incremental safety benefits above and beyond existing donor‐based mitigations (e.g., HLA‐tested female donors, male‐only donors). However, differences between PLT plasma, PLT PAS, and PLT PAS‐PR preparations were no longer statistically significant in the 2017–2023 sub‐analysis (p‐values for pair‐wise comparison about 0.9 for each comparison, Table ). In contrast, with PLT pooled‐related TRALI cases reported between 2017 and 2019, its incidence was 10 (0, 41.7) per million units distributed despite shrinking utilization in that interval. Production of PLT pooled ceased entirely in 2020. 3.3 Model‐based pairwise comparisons To quantify between‐component differences, we fit a mixed‐effects model (fixed effect: component type; random effect: calendar year) and report adjusted absolute risk differences per 10 6 distributions using pooled whole‐blood platelets (PLT pooled) as the index comparator (Table ). Compared with PLT pooled, the risk difference was −10.0 (95% CI −17.4 to −2.6; p = .002) for plasma, −11.5 (−18.9 to −4.0; p = .0002) for RBCs, −9.2 (−16.6 to −1.8; p = .006) for apheresis platelets in 100% plasma, −12.8 (−20.8 to −4.8; p = .0001) for apheresis PAS platelets, and −13.1 (−22.4 to −3.8; p = .001) for apheresis PAS‐PR platelets. Interpreted clinically, these differences correspond to ~9–13 fewer high‐probability TRALI cases per million units when transfusing apheresis‐platelet preparations (or plasma/RBCs) rather than PLT pooled over the full 2006–2023 interval. These findings align with the component‐specific incidences in Table (e.g., 13.6/million for PLT pooled vs. ≤4.4/million for apheresis subtypes). In the post‐mitigation era (2017–2023)—after universal HLA screening of previously pregnant apheresis‐platelet donors and broader use of PAS/PR—the pairwise differences among apheresis subtypes were small and not statistically significant (all adjusted p ≈ 0.9), consistent with a floor effect once donor‐based mitigations and reduced plasma volumes were in place (Table ). By contrast, PLT pooled retained a higher point estimate (10.0 [0, 41.7] per million) despite declining use until production ceased in 2020. 3.4 Donor‐risk profile of pooled whole‐blood platelets Table details the distribution of TRALI risk donors within 538,467 pooled platelet units for which complete donor‐health‐questionnaire data were available. At least one donor reporting a recognized TRALI risk factor (prior pregnancy or transfusion) was present in 9.7% of pools; fully mitigated pools containing zero such donors accounted for 90.3% of distributions. Notably, 3–5 high‐risk donors were present in 2.4% of all pools, underscoring the multiplicative antibody‐exposure potential inherent to this component. In summary, our apheresis‐platelet data suggested that male‐predominant plasma and HLA‐antibody screening of female apheresis‐platelet donors have together reduced plasma‐related TRALI by >90% and apheresis‐platelet‐related TRALI by a further >70%. Nevertheless, pooled whole‐blood platelets—manufactured without analogous donor or manufacturing safeguards—remained the leading residual source of TRALI until their discontinuation in 2020. 4 DISCUSSION Our 18‐year hemovigilance analysis showed a consistently higher TRALI risk with pooled platelets derived from WB than with any other component per million products distributed (13.6/10 6 vs. 4.4/10 6 or less). Although PAS should theoretically lower TRALI by reducing exposure to donor antibodies, our data revealed no meaningful difference in TRALI incidence between PAS platelets and 100% plasma platelets (−3.6/10 6 , p = .9); pathogen‐reduced (PLT PAS‐PR) apheresis platelets likewise showed a nonsignificant decline (−3.9/10 6 , p = .9). These findings imply that donor‐based mitigations already captured most of the achievable risk reduction, leaving little added benefit from simply reducing plasma volume. By contrast, US policy still permits WB‐derived pools of unscreened donors, each contributing ~50 mL of plasma. Every additional donor heightens the chance that at least one high‐titer HLA/HNA antibody enters the pool, explaining the elevated TRALI signal we observe. Canada and France have addressed this threat with two complementary safeguards: (1) a male‐predominant pooling rule that requires at least three of four (Canada) or four of five (France) donors in every pool to be male, and (2) systematic HLA‐antibody screening of female donors whose plasma will enter platelet pools. , Our study's strengths include centralized adjudication of all highly probable and definite TRALI cases, a uniform case definition, and linkage to distribution data for every component type, allowing us to track the real‐world impact of evolving mitigations—male‐only plasma, HLA screening, PAS, and PR—over nearly two decades. This is in contrast to published metanalyses of prevalence reports that often segregate reports on passive versus active but may not distinguish what level of certainty was used to report TRALI numbers and will include reports where low‐probability (i.e., possible) cases were included alongside high probability and definite adjudicated cases. Limitations of our study include reliance on a single national blood organization (albeit one supplying a large share of the US inventory), passive hospital reporting that likely underestimated true TRALI rates and cannot be used to estimate true absolute rates but provided useful information about relative rates and changes in rates over time. Other limitations are exclusion of multicomponent transfusions, and incomplete visibility into patient mix or local surveillance rigor. Manufacturing and transfusion practice also changed across 18 years which further added heterogeneity. The recent FDA approval of the Reveos® system (Terumo BCT)—which automates centrifugation and expression of WB into red cells, plasma, and a concentrated platelet product—has rekindled US interest in WB‐derived platelets. Yet current FDA rules still demand that room‐temperature WB be processed within 8 hours, whereas Canada, France, and several other European nations allow a 24‐hour hold. Adopting a similar 24‐hour window would ease night‐shift staffing, reduce wastage, and make WB platelets operationally more attractive, provided simultaneous safety measures are considered. Suggested safety measures may include: (1) routine HLA/HNA antibody testing of all female platelet donors and (2) a male‐predominant pooling rule—at least four of five donors, or all but one, must meet a mitigation criterion in every pool. These steps mirror the successful approaches in Canada and France. In sum, the marked differential risk between pooled WB and apheresis platelets was likely a true safety signal, not a reporting artifact. Aligning pooled‐platelet safeguards with those already standard for apheresis platelets—and embedding such requirements into any new WB‐platelet workflows—should reduce their TRALI risk. Coupled with ongoing hospital education to recognize and report TRALI, these evidence‐based actions would keep US transfusion practice on par with international best practice and further protect patients from a preventable, potentially fatal reaction. 5 CONCLUSIONS Despite major advances in mitigating TRALI risk for RBC and plasma transfusions—both now characterized by very low incidence rates—our data highlight that WB‐derived pooled platelets remain a significant source of TRALI risk. Reducing plasma volume through PAS or employing pathogen reduction offers only incremental gains over existing donor screening measures, underscoring the critical need to adopt equally stringent mitigation strategies for pooled platelets. Routine HLA/HNA screening and/or using predominantly male donors for pool formation could align safety measures with those already implemented for apheresis platelets, reducing TRALI risk across all platelet components.
